title: VGG – Simplicity in Depth
description: Exploring VGG, the architecture that showed depth and uniform design could improve performance on large-scale image recognition.

body.raw: ## Context & Motivation By 2014, AlexNet had already proven that CNNs could crush image classification when scaled up, and GoogLeNet was experimenting with clever modules to make things efficient. VGG, from the Visual Geometry Group at Oxford (hence the name), took a different path. Instead of being fancy, it asked a simple question: *what if we just make the network deeper, but keep it uniform?* That idea sounds obvious now, but it was powerful. VGG showed that depth alone, combined with small 3×3 filters, could significantly improve performance on ImageNet. This was also one of the first models that people outside research used heavily for transfer learning, since its structure was clean and easy to adapt. When I first learned about VGG in class, it was presented as the "clean" architecture. It looked boring compared to GoogLeNet or ResNet, but that’s what made it so influential. The simplicity was its strength. ## Model Breakdown The most popular versions are **VGG16** and **VGG19**, where the numbers stand for how many weight layers they have. The structure looks repetitive, but that was the point: stack small 3×3 convolutions, add a pooling layer, repeat, and then finish with a few fully connected layers. Here’s the pattern for **VGG16**: - Input: 224×224 RGB image - Conv3-64 → Conv3-64 → MaxPool - Conv3-128 → Conv3-128 → MaxPool - Conv3-256 → Conv3-256 → Conv3-256 → MaxPool - Conv3-512 → Conv3-512 → Conv3-512 → MaxPool - Conv3-512 → Conv3-512 → Conv3-512 → MaxPool - FC-4096 → FC-4096 → FC-1000 (softmax) The main differences from AlexNet: - All conv filters are 3×3 with stride 1, padding 1 - Pooling is always 2×2 with stride 2 - Deeper, more consistent design (16–19 layers) --- ## Why the Design Choices Matter **3×3 convolutions** Stacking two 3×3 convs gives you the receptive field of a 5×5 filter, but with fewer parameters and more non-linearities. This made the network expressive without exploding in size. **Depth** Before VGG, CNNs were usually under 10 layers. VGG pushed this to 16 and 19 layers, showing that deeper really was better (as long as you had data and compute). **Uniform design** Because every block looked the same, it was easy to reason about and extend. This is why VGG quickly became a go-to backbone for other tasks like detection and segmentation. --- ## Implementation Notes Here’s a simplified PyTorch version of VGG16: ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn class VGG16(nn.Module): def __init__(self, num_classes=1000): super(VGG16, self).__init__() self.features = nn.Sequential( # Block 1 nn.Conv2d(3, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.Conv2d(64, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.MaxPool2d(2, 2), # Block 2 nn.Conv2d(64, 128, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.Conv2d(128, 128, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.MaxPool2d(2, 2), # Block 3 nn.Conv2d(128, 256, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.Conv2d(256, 256, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.Conv2d(256, 256, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.MaxPool2d(2, 2), # Block 4 nn.Conv2d(256, 512, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.Conv2d(512, 512, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.Conv2d(512, 512, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.MaxPool2d(2, 2), # Block 5 nn.Conv2d(512, 512, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.Conv2d(512, 512, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.Conv2d(512, 512, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.MaxPool2d(2, 2), ) self.classifier = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(512 * 7 * 7, 4096), nn.ReLU(True), nn.Dropout(), nn.Linear(4096, 4096), nn.ReLU(True), nn.Dropout(), nn.Linear(4096, num_classes), ) def forward(self, x): x = self.features(x) x = x.view(x.size(0), -1) x = self.classifier(x) return x ``` Training VGG was much more computationally expensive than AlexNet. It highlighted the need for faster GPUs and more memory. Despite that, it became hugely popular in research, especially for transfer learning on smaller datasets. ## Reflections What I like about VGG is how straightforward it is. Compared to GoogLeNet’s Inception modules or ResNet’s skip connections, VGG is just stack, pool, stack, pool. That simplicity made it a great teaching model and a backbone for lots of other tasks. Of course, it came at a cost. VGG16 has about 138 million parameters, which is huge compared to modern networks. It’s heavy and not very efficient. But it proved the point: depth and uniform design worked. Later models built on this lesson. ResNet solved the training difficulties that came with even deeper networks. EfficientNet explored better scaling rules. Transformers went in a totally new direction. But VGG’s fingerprint is still visible in many of them: small filters, repeated blocks, and the idea that simple can sometimes beat clever.
